rows.text:
Fever: Scaling Culture from Madrid to the World
')">
Sep 20, 2026
5min read
Fever: Scaling Culture from Madrid to the World
Fever: Scaling Culture from Madrid to the World
Authors
Carolina Brochado
Ludwig Scherm
Shariq Varawalla
William Evensen
Kanak Sharma
While much of the technology industry is focused on what AI might replace, Fever has spent more than a decade building technology for something it cannot: the energy of a live crowd and the memory of an experience shared with other people.
Founded by Spanish entrepreneurs, Fever has grown into a global technology platform powering live entertainment across more than 55 countries and 500 cities. Today, it helps venues, promoters, artists, sports organisations and cultural institutions understand audiences, generate demand, sell tickets and make successful experiences around the world. Today, Fever powers frictionless and discoverable access to famous cultural icons such as the Palace of Versailles, the Royal Palace of Madrid and leading sport events and teams such as F1, SailGP, FC Barcelona and Atlético de Madrid. Essentially, Fever helps more people access and experience culture across Europe and beyond.
We’re excited to announce that the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, is leading Fever’s $250 million primary equity financing round, alongside Point72 Private Investments, Baillie Gifford and other existing investors.
Ignacio Bachiller,  Francisco Hein and Alexandre Pérez, co-founders of Fever:
“We’ve always believed that you can build a global technology leader from Europe without compromising on ambition. Today we already operate in more than 55 countries, but there is still so much more to build. The Scaleup Europe Fund represents something important for European founders: the ability to access meaningful capital at home when the opportunity becomes truly global. We’re proud to be part of that story, and excited about what we can build together from here.”
Technology for the experience economy
“
Today, we reaffirm that culture is the soul of Europe, and its greatest strength
.”
Ursula von der Leyen, European cultural declaration, 2026.
Culture and live entertainment are part of the social fabric of cities around the world, yet much of the technology behind that economy has historically focused on the transaction, helping people buy a ticket once they already know what they want to see. Fever started somewhere else: with discovery and demand.
Over time, that has allowed the company to build an increasingly powerful technology and data layer across the entire experience economy. Its platform now spans discovery, demand generation, ticketing, pricing and event operations. Underneath it sits a proprietary data engine bringing together trillions of data points about how consumers discover and engage with experiences.
That data creates a powerful flywheel, helping Fever understand and grow audiences, optimise pricing and marketing, and identify where successful concepts can travel next. AI makes that engine increasingly powerful across campaign automation, pricing, discovery and partner products.
The result is something increasingly different from a traditional ticketing business. We see Fever becoming a technology infrastructure layer, and ultimately an important operating system for live entertainment.
“
It’s culture that cements European identity.”
Umberto Eco.
Built in Madrid, scaling globally
Europe has produced successful technology companies, but creating them is only half the challenge. The other half is enabling them to keep scaling when the opportunity becomes truly global.
Fever is showing what that can look like. It reaches hundreds of millions of consumers across culture, entertainment and sport.
Companies that reach this scale can create a flywheel around them: They can build and attract new talent, compound expertise and experience, shape the ecosystems around them, and create our next generation of founders.
We have seen this with Spotify, whose alumni have gone on to build dozens of new companies around the ecosystem in which it was built.
We believe Fever can have that kind of impact for Madrid, Spain and Europe, and that is core to the Scaleup Europe Fund’s mission: helping European leaders go global, while staying European. Founders should be able to build from Europe, all the way.
The next chapter
Live entertainment represents hundreds of billions of dollars in consumer spending, yet remains fragmented across markets and legacy technology platforms. We believe Fever’s global distribution, proprietary data, AI and operating capabilities can help shape the industry’s next generation.
And EQT can bring more than capital to that journey. Our teams will work alongside Fever across international expansion, commercial partnerships, AI and product, talent and, over time, the capital markets, drawing on EQT’s global network and experience scaling technology businesses.
Carolina Brochado, Partner at EQT:
"
We're incredibly excited to back this exceptional founder-led team out of Spain that has built a strong operating system for live entertainment - from discovery and demand generation to ticketing and on-site operations. Fever has built core infrastructure that powers and scales culture. We've enjoyed tracking Fever for years and believe the team is building one of Europe's defining technology companies. They are now operating at a global scale, and we're excited to now help support them on their journey
."
Fever began with a simple idea of helping people discover more of the world around them.
Today, that idea has become a global technology company helping power how millions of people experience culture in the physical world.
We’re proud to back Ignacio, Francisco, Alexandre and the entire Fever team as they take that journey from Madrid to the world.
This is a marketing communication. Please refer to the information document of the Scaleup Europe Fund before making any final investment decisions.

rows.title: EUCLYD’s €200M Series A to stop moving data
rows.text:
EUCLYD’s €200M Series A to stop moving data
')">
Sep 14, 2026
5min read
EUCLYD’s €200M Series A to stop moving data
EUCLYD’s €200M Series A to stop moving data
Authors
Ted Persson
Saiteja Sriramagiri
Founded in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, EUCLYD is raising over €200 million, co-led by Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, Samsung Catalyst Fund, Somerset Capital Partners, and Innovation Industries.
We are investing because the economics of AI are moving from training to inference, while the hardware stack was built for the former.
“Europe has spent decades building some of the world's deepest semiconductor and systems-engineering expertise. What companies like EUCLYD need now is the ambition and capital to turn that foundation into globally competitive technology companies. The Scaleup Europe Fund brings both the scale of investment and the long-term European perspective that makes it a particularly strong partner for the journey we're embarking on.”
Bernardo Kastrup, Founder and CEO, EUCLYD
In 1977, accepting the Turing Award, John Backus spent much of his lecture complaining about a tube. The tube connected a processor to its memory and could carry one word at a time. He called it the von Neumann bottleneck.
Forty-nine years later, the tube is wider and the processor is a GPU. The complaint still stands. Moving data out of memory costs far more energy than doing arithmetic on it. For decades, this was an engineering tax. At inference scale, it becomes a gross-margin problem.
Training is how a model gets made. It is experimental: architectures change, runs fail, and nobody knows in March what researchers will want to try in June. Flexibility is worth paying for. GPUs won this market because they can run almost anything thrown at them, and they deserved to.
Inference is how a model gets used. Once deployed, the weights are largely fixed, the computation becomes more predictable, and the same model may answer millions of requests each day. Every token consumes memory bandwidth, rack capacity and power. The cost lands directly in the economics of the product.
Thousands of short tubes
Craftwerk, EUCLYD's inference system, takes a different approach. Instead of placing a large pool of memory behind a small number of general-purpose processors, it repeats one simple unit across one of the physically largest AI accelerators built to date: a small processor, its own local DRAM and its own connection to the rest of the system.
The point is not that data stops moving entirely. It moves less far, through fewer shared bottlenecks and on a schedule the machine can know in advance. Data for the next operation can arrive while the current one runs. Large models make the problem worse. The weights need bandwidth. The growing context cache needs capacity. The largest production models must be spread across many accelerators, which then have to coordinate continuously.
EUCLYD is trying to keep a model within one tightly integrated system, rather than distributing it across a network of separate accelerator servers. Memory sits beside the processors that use it. Each processor has a known role in a static schedule. The next batch can be fetched while the current one computes.
The architecture is built for high-volume inference, where the winning metric is not a spectacular single-query demo but the cost of serving billions of tokens.
Groq and Cerebras have validated market demand for alternatives to GPU-centric inference. EUCLYD is targeting the entire inference market, from ultra-low-latency applications to cost-sensitive, throughput-heavy workloads where batching, rack efficiency and tokens per watt determine margin.
The right shape, in the right decade
Danny Hillis's Connection Machine, built in the 1980s, had 65,536 processors, each with its own memory. Inmos's Transputer, developed in Bristol during the same period, combined processing, memory and communication links in a tileable design. Both had the right shape and the wrong decade.
Today's inference workloads are repetitive in a way few large-scale computations have been before. The same weights are read again and again. The same operations are run across new batches of tokens. That predictability makes specialisation more valuable.
The manufacturing stack has also changed. Custom memory, advanced packaging and wafer-to-wafer bonding make it possible to place far more memory much closer to compute than those earlier machines could.
And the economics are less forgiving. AI companies increasingly evaluate the cost of the whole system: accelerators, memory, networking, cooling, rack space and power. For many new deployments, access to power is becoming as constraining as access to chips. Every watt spent moving data is a watt that cannot serve another token.
Hyperscalers have already responded by moving more AI workloads onto their own silicon. They can afford to build around their own models, infrastructure and utilisation patterns. Most companies cannot. They still need an independent platform.
The people: the Avengers of silicon
Long-time collaborators Bernardo Kastrup and Atul Sinha first co-founded Silicon Hive at Philips Research, later acquired by Intel, before reuniting to found EUCLYD. Kastrup later led product strategy at ASML.
Co-founders Gerard Egelmeers, Ingolf Held and Harm Peters have worked alongside Kastrup and Sinha for more than two decades across Philips NatLab, Silicon Hive and Intel. Together, they have designed and taped out multiple generations of parallel processors.
Peter Wennink, who led ASML from 2013 to 2024, chairs the board. Federico Faggin, designer of the Intel 4004, advises the company.
Kastrup also has a second life as a philosopher. His theory of analytic idealism argues that mind is fundamental and that computation, however sophisticated, is not consciousness. He would be the first to say these chips do not think.
What has to be true
This is a silicon bet, focused on maintaining the pace at which AI is iterating.
EUCLYD's first test chip was manufactured at Samsung and will validate the company's compute architecture.
Backus's tube never disappeared. We made it wider, faster and more expensive. EUCLYD is betting that inference does not need an even wider one. It needs thousands of shorter ones, with memory placed beside the computation it serves.
We are making that bet with them.

Tandem Health: Bringing European Healthcare into the AI Era

5min read
Tandem Health: Bringing European Healthcare into the AI Era
Tandem Health: Bringing European Healthcare into the AI Era
Authors
Nils Petter Nygaard
Carolina Brochado
Suki Nahl
Francesca Campbell
Today, we're excited to announce that the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, is leading Tandem Health's $100 million Series B, with participation from existing investors Kinnevik, Northzone, Amino Collective and Visionaries.
Tandem Health is the Fund's first investment in healthcare AI. The capital aims to support Tandem Health in deepening its position as the AI partner to some of Europe's leading care providers, including growing its team of c. 100+ in-house clinicians and expanding its AI medical assistant across more of the clinical workflow, towards an AI-native clinic operating system.
Why we're backing Tandem
Tandem Health is the kind of company the Scaleup Europe Fund was created to back: a European technology company addressing a critical challenge, already demonstrating an ability to scale across highly fragmented markets, with the ambition to build a global leader from Europe. Today, Tandem is used by more than 10,000 care organisations across 14 European markets, navigating different healthcare systems, languages, regulatory regimes and clinical workflows.
For Tandem, the partnership is also about having European scale-up capital behind that ambition. As  Lukas Saari, CEO and Co-Founder, puts it:
“European healthcare works differently, and AI need to be native, rather than retrofitted from other markets. That is what we are building at Tandem. As we continue expanding across Europe, we are proud to have European capital behind us through the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT. This funding allows us to help bring healthcare safely into the AI era, working in tandem with patients, clinicians, systems and nations. We believe Europe should be setting the standard for how AI enters healthcare, not adopting someone else's.”
Less time on documentation, more time with patients
The pressure on Europe's health systems is structural. The WHO estimates Europe was short of around 1.6 million health and social care workers in 2024 and expects that gap to reach 4 million by 2030, alongside an ageing population and a shrinking working-age population to care for it. No health system can close a gap of that size through hiring alone. The variable that can still move is how much of a clinician's day goes to patients rather than to administration. Time spent typing up a consultation is time not spent with patients.
This is where AI can help. Mario Draghi recently argued in the Financial Times that faster AI adoption could become one of Europe's most important levers for productivity growth; in healthcare, where skilled clinical capacity is already constrained, the potential impact is particularly tangible. An AI assistant can listen to the consultation and draft the structured note, suggest the diagnosis and procedure codes, and draft the referral letter or sick note afterwards. Work that used to be done during the appointment or at the end of the day happens in the background, and the clinician's job becomes reviewing and approving rather than typing. Given how high the stakes are in healthcare, the companies that succeed will likely need both product quality, meaning output that is accurate and reflects how clinicians in each market and specialty actually work, and the compliance and safety that health systems require.
Embracing the complexity: Certified clinical AI for regulated markets
European healthcare is complex, fragmented and heavily regulated. It is not one market but many, each with its own health system, language, coding framework and procurement rules. Patient data is among the most sensitive that exists and many AI use cases in clinical settings fall under medical device regulation, so providers cannot adopt a tool simply because it works well; it also has to meet the requirements of the market it is used in.
Tandem Health has been designed for this from the outset. Its AI medical assistant supports clinicians before, during and after the patient visit, and it is the only one whose AI Scribe, Coding Assistant and Clinical Decision Support are each certified as Class IIa medical devices under the EU Medical Device Regulation. It integrates with more than 130 medical record systems across Europe, working with the systems clinics already have.
Behind the product is a founding team that pairs healthcare depth with AI experience: Lukas Saari, Oscar Boldt-Christmas and Oliver Åstrand, between them bringing machine learning backgrounds from Spotify and Google, alongside decades of healthcare experience at McKinsey. They are supported by an in-house team of c. 100 clinicians, helping to develop and deliver the product to the level clinicians require across markets and specialties.
Adopted across Europe, expanding across the entire workflow
Founded in Stockholm in 2023, Tandem Health is today used by more than 10,000 care organisations across 14 European markets, including Ramsay Santé, Capio and the NHS, making it one of few healthcare technology companies to have shown it can scale across European borders.
Clinicians using Tandem Health already spend close to 30% less time on administration and report lower stress and higher job satisfaction, and we believe that impact will only increase as the product expands across more of the clinician's daily workflows. A scribe that captures the whole consultation is a natural base to build from, and coding and clinical decision support are live today. Over time, Tandem Health intends to extend into the wider clinical and administrative workflow towards an AI-native operating system for the clinic, with each step returning more time to clinicians and their patients.
We're excited to partner with Lukas, Oscar, Oliver and the entire Tandem Health team as they help bring European healthcare into the AI era.
*This is a marketing communication. Please refer to the information document of the Scaleup Europe Fund before making any final investment decisions.*

rows.title: Backing The Exploration Company: Building the European Rails for Space Access
rows.text:
Backing The Exploration Company: Building the European Rails for Space Access
')">
Sep 8, 2026
5min read
Backing The Exploration Company: Building the European Rails for Space Access
Backing The Exploration Company: Building the European Rails for Space Access
Authors
Ted Persson
Ludwig Scherm
Saiteja Sriramagiri
Alex Kitsberg
Hampus Särnbratt
In 1980 Europe founded the world's first commercial space launch company. Arianespace was selling rides to orbit four years before the United States passed the law that let its own private companies compete, and by the 1990s Ariane 4 carried half the world's commercial launch market. Europe landed the first probe on Titan and the first on a comet. It built the largest cargo vehicle ever to service the International Space Station, and named the first one Jules Verne. The four that followed were Kepler, Amaldi, Einstein and Lemaître. Five flights between 2008 and 2014, five successes.
Then it stopped. Hermes, the crewed spaceplane, was cancelled in 1992 before it flew. The cargo programme was retired in 2015 and its technology traded into the service module of NASA's Orion capsule, to cover Europe's share of the station's running costs. Europe has never put a person into orbit on a vehicle of its own. It invented commercial launch and never built the company that scaled it.
One of them, who worked on that Orion service module, was Hélène Huby.
In Dune, nothing crosses between worlds except inside the Spacing Guild's ships. The Emperor has the most feared army in the universe, the Great Houses have planets, wealth and soldiers of their own, and none of it moves an inch without the Guild. So the Guild answers to nobody, charges everybody, and the Emperor asks it for passage like anyone else. Power in that universe runs on transport, not on armies. That is not a complaint about the people who kept theirs. Space has always run on partners. The question is what Europe brings to the partnership next.
Because the next space station is not one station but several, all commercial, most of them American, and every one of them needs cargo up and, for anything worth making in orbit, cargo back down. Today almost all of that traffic would go through a single company. We believe no station operator wants one supplier for its lifeline, whatever flag it flies, and neither do the governments buying space on board. We see global demand, and believe there is room for a second ship.The demand is global.
Nyx is that second ship. Europe is building it because Europe needs one. But a second ship changes the terms for everyone who has been negotiating with one, in Houston as much as in Paris.
The Exploration Company
The company building Nyx is The Exploration Company, founded by Hélène Huby in 2021.
Hélène didn't grow up wanting to build spaceships. She studied economics and applied mathematics and ended up in space, as she puts it, more or less by chance. She joined Airbus in Germany in 2013, fell in love with the industry, and went on to work across ArianeGroup, Airbus's space strategy and eventually the European Service Module for NASA's Orion spacecraft.
It gave her a unique view of European space. Europe had extraordinary engineers and decades of experience building things that actually flew. Her own team was helping build the spacecraft that would take humans back towards the Moon. But Europe had stopped building its own way of getting people and cargo to and from orbit.
Hélène thought it could do more.
While at Airbus, she started to think about what could be next. Ultimately, she was joined by a small team of like-minded aerospace veterans, including Artur Koop, Jon Reijneveld, Pierre Vinet and Sebastien Reichstadt. They worked on weekends. Hélène checked herself into a hotel in Germany for three days with a spreadsheet to figure out whether any of this could actually become a business.
The spreadsheet said maybe. And that was enough.
In August 2021, they left and started The Exploration Company.
There’s some history here too. The EQT Ventures team first backed he Exploration Company in its early days. Over dinner in Paris in 2022, Hélène explained how Nyx, and the launcher she planned to build next, would work using her mobile phone and a water glass.
Four months later, EQT Ventures co-led The Exploration Company's €40.5 million Series A. We backed Hélène again in the €150 million Series B in 2024.
Since then, The Exploration Company has turned into a company of close to 600 people across Europe, the US and the UAE, building Nyx and a much bigger transportation system around it.
Today we're doubling down on Hélène and the team (quadrupling down technically?). The $450 million Series C is co-led by the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, alongside Atomico and Bessemer.
The master plan
The plan is simple (definitely not rocket science or anything like that):
Build a reusable capsule.
Use its customers, cash flow and technology to master the full transportation stack, starting with a high-thrust engine
Use cost-competitive, frequent transport to build the services that run on top of it.
The Exploration Company’s goal is to create a space economy that isn't monopolised by a few and imported by everyone else.
Step one: the Nyx Capsule
Nyx is a reusable spacecraft designed to carry roughly three tonnes to orbit and back.
It can dock with a crewed station, return valuable cargo safely, and fly on European, American, Indian or Japanese rockets. TEC sells the mission rather than the launch: delivery, docking, return and recovery.
That lets TEC own the customer before it owns the rocket.
Step two: the engine and the rocket
Nyx creates revenue, flight heritage and a customer base. It also forces TEC to master the systems needed for larger vehicles.
Storm, TEC’s reusable methane-oxygen engine, will power a reusable heavy launcher designed for station modules, constellation batches and defence infrastructure.
It needs to become a credible independent option for Europe, sovereign customers and commercial operators.
Step three: the things that run on it
Cheap, frequent transport is what makes orbital compute, in-space manufacturing and sovereign communications viable. Europe has watched this sequence once already, in AI, and is now paying to build the layer it skipped. Space is the same shape, a decade earlier. Maybe asteroid mining. Maybe a Mars Base. Who knows?
The ships between worlds
The idea is pretty simple: Europe should have a ship.
Not because every continent needs its own version of every technology company. And not because SpaceX isn't very good at what it does.
But if you want to build things in space, it could help not to depend on one company to get you there.
That is what we like about The Exploration Company. Nyx is European, but the business doesn't have to be. It can launch on an American rocket, dock with an American station and carry cargo for customers anywhere in the world.
Europe gets its own way to space. Everyone else gets another option.
Which brings us back to
Dune
.
The Spacing Guild figured out that you don't actually need to own the planets if you own the ships between them.
We don't expect Hélène to start wearing an enormous orange helmet.
But we do think she is building the ships.
And there is an enormous amount left to build. Space is hard. Rockets explode. Re-entry is unforgiving. Certification takes years. Building one spacecraft is difficult; building a company that routinely flies them, then a reusable rocket, is something else entirely.
There will be delays, failed tests, things that need rebuilding and probably a few plans that look quite different by the time they reach orbit.
That comes with the territory.
Kennedy's old line still works: we do these things “not because they are easy, but because they are hard.”
Hélène and the team have picked something very hard.
We're very happy to be backing them for the journey.
Godspeed, TEC.
*This is a marketing communication. Please refer to the information document of the Scaleup Europe Fund before making any final investment decisions.*

rows.title: Mistral AI: Europe's Full-Stack AI Champion
rows.text:
Mistral AI: Europe's Full-Stack AI Champion
')">
Sep 8, 2026
5min read
Mistral AI: Europe's Full-Stack AI Champion
Mistral AI: Europe's Full-Stack AI Champion
Authors
Kirk Lepke
Shannee Braun
Marcel Goehre
Juliette Quellec
Kanak Sharma
Today, we're excited to announce that the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, is co-leading Mistral AI's €3.0 billion Series D at more than €21 billion post-money valuation, together with Samsung. It is the largest equity fundraising ever completed by a European technology company, three years after the company's launch. The round will fund deeper frontier research, expanded infrastructure and accelerated international growth.
Our investment in Mistral is the Fund’s third, and a clear expression of what the Scaleup Europe Fund was created to do: make sure Europe's strategic technology companies can scale with meaningful European capital supporting them.
A large market at its inflection point, shifting toward control and trust
The central question in AI is shifting: from who can build the most powerful model, to how can organisations harness frontier AI without surrendering control. Especially in critical industries, companies and organisations have always been sensitive to where their technology comes from and how it is operated. Recent US export restrictions on frontier models are further reinforcing demand for sovereign AI solutions that they can trust with their most sensitive data. At the same time, rising frontier token costs are fuelling demand for lower-cost models customised to specific use cases, and boards and shareholders are pushing hard to turn AI pilots into real adoption in production, in large enterprises as much as in the public sector.
Our thesis is simple: the addressable market for AI built on control and trust – while already sizeable – is at a clear inflection point and will see rapid acceleration over the coming years. Serving it requires what few have: talent to build models at the frontier, deep domain expertise to help customers turn AI into real business value, and access to sovereign compute at scale.
Mistral: the full-stack champion of sovereign AI under customer control
Mistral is building on exactly those pillars to become the leading provider of full-stack AI solutions for the most complex and mission-critical use cases.
Founded in Paris in 2023 by Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix – a world-class ex-DeepMind and Meta team. Mistral is Europe's leading frontier AI lab and home to one of the strongest AI research teams in the world, which we believe is a decisive advantage in a talent-scarce field. Its approach has been consistent from the start: open-weight frontier models built with strong capital efficiency. Today that means open frontier models alongside a family of smaller, specialised ones (coding, documents, speech) and, because the weights are open, customers can run, adapt and fine-tune them on their own infrastructure, with their own data, and never locked into a single vendor's roadmap, pricing or availability.
Expanding beyond models, Mistral has built the delivery capabilities most AI companies lack. Forward-deployed engineers embed inside customer teams to scope the high-value use cases, integrate Mistral's models and platform into existing systems, and fine-tune them on the customer's proprietary data. It is the difference between a pilot and a system a business actually runs on, and it is how truly complex problems get solved: engineers who understand the model working next to people who understand the business. Success in one workflow then expands across teams and use cases, deepening each account over time.
The third layer is compute. Mistral is building its own European infrastructure – targeting a gigawatt of capacity in Europe over the next few years, aimed to be Europe's largest AI campus outside of Paris. Access to EU-based, sovereign compute can allow customers to further reduce dependency on US hyperscalers while choosing where their intelligence runs. It is the boundary inside which an organisation's most valuable data, workflows and institutional knowledge can compound privately.
In our view the combination of these layers drives a real flywheel, with each layer strengthening the others. Open-weight models lower the barrier to adoption for regulated buyers; forward-deployed engineers turn pilots into production systems, and success expands across teams and use cases; every deployment generates operational intelligence and reusable solutions that improve the models and shorten the delivery cycle; and owned compute improves the economics of everything above it. That compounding is the heart of our thesis – the platform can improve as it scales. Now with 125+ customers across 20 countries, Mistral is being adopted where the bar is high, including some of the largest enterprises and public institutions across financial services, manufacturing, healthcare, defence and critical infrastructure.
Global ambition, European roots: core to the mandate of the Scaleup Europe Fund
We believe that Europe can create technology companies at the global frontier. But when they scale, the capital – and with it the ownership – has come from outside Europe. From 2013 to 2023, 82 percent of scale-up deals in the EU involved a foreign lead investor, according to data from the European Investment Bank. The Scaleup Europe Fund is here with the aim to change that. It exists so that founders with global ambition can keep strong European roots.
Europe needs not only the talent to build frontier AI companies, but the capital to remain at the table as they scale globally. AI makes that point sharper than any other sector: it is increasingly tied to economic competitiveness, to infrastructure, and to technological capability itself.
EQT, managing the Scaleup Europe Fund, also brings more than capital. Through the platform, Mistral gains access to one of the world's largest data centre franchises and deep infrastructure expertise, customer and partner introductions across Europe, the US and Asia, and capital markets experience for the next phase of its build-out.
We're excited to partner with Arthur, Guillaume, Timothée and the entire Mistral team as they build what we believe can become a generational European company – and a global leader.

Heart Aerospace completes first flight of the world's largest electric aircraft
Heart Aerospace completes first flight of the world's largest electric aircraft
Authors
EQT Ventures
Heart Aerospace has reached a major milestone on the path to commercial electric aviation by successfully completing the first flight of its X1 demonstrator: the largest battery-electric aircraft ever to take to the skies.
The piloted test flight took place at Plattsburgh International Airport in New York and demonstrated all-electric flight at a scale relevant to commercial airline operations. With a wingspan of 106 feet and a takeoff weight exceeding 25,000 pounds, the X1 represents a significant step toward Heart's ES-30, a 30-seat hybrid-electric regional aircraft targeted to enter service in 2031.
The milestone validates key technologies that will underpin the ES-30, which has already attracted orders and options from airlines including United Airlines, Air Canada and JSX. According to Heart, the aircraft is designed to reduce operating costs by more than 40% compared with today's regional aircraft through lower energy costs, simplified electric propulsion and a software-defined architecture.
Congratulations to Anders Forslund and the entire Heart Aerospace team on an extraordinary achievement, and an important step toward making cleaner, more affordable regional air travel a reality.

Why the Scaleup Europe Fund is Backing Lovable's Next Chapter

Why the Scaleup Europe Fund is Backing Lovable's Next Chapter
Why the Scaleup Europe Fund is Backing Lovable's Next Chapter
Authors
Victor Englesson
Sandra Malmberg
Nils Petter Nygaard
Today, we're excited to share that the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, is co-leading Lovable's $400 million Series C alongside Menlo Ventures, at a $13.3 billion valuation.
After first backing Lovable in its Series B in December 2025, we're deepening our partnership with one of the fastest-moving companies in European technology, and one that represents exactly what the Scaleup Europe Fund was created to support: exceptional European founders building a category-defining technology company with global ambition.
The round also broadens Lovable's investor base, with new backers joining from Europe, Latin America, Asia and the US, a group as international as the company itself.
Why Lovable
The best business ideas come from the people closest to the problem. They belong to the operator who has run the same broken process for years, the entrepreneur who knows exactly what their customers need, and the founder who understands a market from the inside. Until now, turning that knowledge into software meant raising capital, hiring engineers and waiting months for a first version, a bar high enough that many ideas were never tested at all.
Lovable removes these constraints. Anyone can describe what they want in plain language and get back a production-grade application: no code, no engineering team, no upfront capital. The idea is the only requirement.
The response has been remarkable: more than 60 million projects built in under two years, over 900 million monthly visits to what's been created, and most builders working on a business they intend to monetise, many already earning revenue.
The same shift is underway inside large enterprises. Employees at nearly two-thirds of the Fortune 500 now build with Lovable, while companies including Adidas, NVIDIA and Deutsche Telekom are using it to create software around their own workflows and rethink the tools their teams rely on.
From Creation Tool to Operating Platform
For most people building on Lovable, the app is just the starting point, the goal is a business that wins customers and earns revenue.
Lovable is now meeting builders across that journey, adding payments, discoverability, integrations and enterprise-grade security and governance, and evolving into a platform on which businesses can increasingly be created and run end to end.
In the UK, a founder built a fashion app without writing a line of code and has grown it to hundreds of thousands of customers. In Brazil, an entrepreneur runs an entire education company on Lovable, including its CRM, finance and sales workflows.
Lovable's position also allows it to benefit from advances across the AI ecosystem. It sits above individual models, orchestrating several frontier models and using the right one for each task, so improvements across the underlying technology can flow into the product.
At the same time, tens of millions of projects give Lovable an increasingly rich understanding of what people build and what succeeds. Each successful product has the potential to make the system better for the next builder.
Built in Europe. Scaling Globally.
Lovable is also a powerful example of what is happening in European technology.
Europe has no shortage of exceptional founders, breakthrough technology or global ambition. The challenge comes when its most successful companies reach the scale-up stage.
At that point, European companies have historically relied heavily on US growth capital. Global capital is an important part of building global companies, and Lovable's new investor base reflects that. But Europe also needs investors with the scale and ambition to continue backing its best companies as they grow. That's the gap the Scaleup Europe Fund was established to help address.
The objective isn't to keep European companies focused on Europe. It's to give founders greater choice: the ability to remain independent, continue taking risks and build global category leaders while maintaining strong roots in Europe.
And capital is only part of that equation. Through EQT's global platform, Lovable can access customers, experienced operators, advisors, industrial expertise and long-term capital as it scales. Companies across EQT's portfolio are already building with Lovable: from product teams shipping applications while engineering resources are constrained, to teams creating their own tools reducing or even eliminating software costs, and shaping how they actually work.
Lovable remains anchored in Stockholm while building hubs in London, Boston, San Francisco and New York. European roots and global ambition can, and should, go hand in hand.
We're incredibly proud to deepen our partnership with Anton, Fabian and the entire Lovable team as they build the platform for the next generation of businesses.

rows.title: Backing Dwelly: Building the AI-native End-to-End Platform for Property Management
rows.text:
Backing Dwelly: Building the AI-native End-to-End Platform for Property Management
')">
Jul 28, 2026
5min read
Backing Dwelly: Building the AI-native End-to-End Platform for Property Management
Backing Dwelly: Building the AI-native End-to-End Platform for Property Management
Authors
Nils Petter Nygaard
Marcel Goehre
Alex Kitsberg
Our investment
Dwelly raises $170 million Series B to build the AI operating system for the lettings market.
EQT Growth is co-leading the round alongside existing investor General Catalyst.
We couldn't be more excited to back founders Ilya Drozdov, Dan Lifshits and Dmitry Khanukov as they build what we believe can become the defining end-to-end platform in one of the largest, most fragmented and most underserved service markets in the UK.
Why we're backing applied-AI services roll-ups
One of our highest-conviction themes in EQT Growth over the past year has been what we call
applied-AI services roll-ups
.
The idea is simple. All across the economy there are big, fragmented, labour-heavy service industries that have barely changed in decades. The usual way to build value here is traditional buy-and-build: acquire lots of small businesses at low multiples and bolt them together into something larger. Most of the value comes from scale and multiple arbitrage.
We think AI changes that picture in a meaningful way. In the right markets, modern AI can automate a big chunk of the manual, repetitive work that runs these businesses. That opens up a different kind of value creation: real, structural margin expansion that comes from genuinely transforming how the business operates, not from financial engineering. People are freed from admin to do the things that actually grow the business, like winning new customers and cross-selling. And because every acquisition adds proprietary longitudinal data from the system of action (long-term records of human services interaction that can be leveraged for AI agentic execution), the automation keeps getting better as the platform grows: a data flywheel and a first-mover edge that compound with scale.
Put simply, as the models improve, automation deepens across mundane admin tasks, thereby freeing up resources to focus on driving growth. The platform gets better the bigger it gets and increased scale drives material margin expansion.
Not every market suits this. The sweet spot combines deep fragmentation, recurring and resilient revenue, workflows that are genuinely automatable, and a customer base with little reason to bring the work in-house. UK property management ticks every one of those boxes, and we think Dwelly is the best-placed team to go after it.
Why Dwelly fits our thesis
A big, resilient and deeply fragmented market
UK residential lettings run on recurring, contracted revenue. Property managers earn a take-rate on rent, and the rent roll sitting underneath the UK private rented sector runs into the tens of billions of pounds a year. With industry gross retention of around 90–95%, that income is unusually sticky and largely shrugs off the economic cycle. It's a material addressable market with clear structural growth tailwinds, as rising regulatory and compliance demands push more landlords toward professional management.
It's also remarkably fragmented. There are more than 10,000 letting agencies in the UK, most of them independent and owner-run, with no scaled player holding meaningful shares. That long tail, plus a steady wave of owner retirements and successions creates a deep, durable pipeline of targets, the bulk of which sit well below the radar of larger consolidators. And the typical customer is a landlord with just a handful of properties – a group that simply can't manage professionally in-house, and is increasingly happy to outsource it.
In other words, it's exactly the kind of resilient, recurring, fragmented market where an applied-AI roll-up can compound for years.
Tech- and AI-first: not multiple arbitrage
What sets Dwelly apart from a typical roll-up is that the engine of value creation is operational, not financial.
The team has built a proprietary platform from the ground up, its own CRM and an end-to-end agentic workflow layer, purpose-built to automate the work of a lettings agency: finding tenants, managing properties, and collecting rent. The difference shows. Jobs that used to take weeks now take days, tenant placement and issue resolution happen far faster, and the earliest, most fully integrated agencies are running at EBITDA margins several times higher than the ~10–15% typical of traditional operators.
When Dwelly buys an agency, it keeps the local brand, the staff and the customer relationships, so nothing changes for landlords, while moving the back office onto its platform and absorbing natural staff turnover through automation rather than blunt cost-cutting. Every deal also feeds Dwelly's proprietary dataset, widening the gap over both legacy incumbents and any would-be new entrant.
This is really the heart of it. Traditional roll-ups buy cheap and lever up. Dwelly buys, transforms, and compounds.
A founder team we have huge conviction in
We've rarely been as impressed by a team's depth of operational understanding.
Ilya, Dan and Dmitry are exactly the profile this thesis calls for, fast-scaling operators from businesses like Uber and Gett, with prior experience building tech-enabled property businesses, and a culture our advisors repeatedly described as "execution machines" with seriously high talent density.
But what really sold us was how they went about it. Before writing a line of code, the team moved to Hull for 18 months to run a property management agency themselves — living the daily reality of letting agents, landlords, tenants and contractors. That immersion became the foundation for the platform they built. Instead of dropping software on an industry from the outside, they encoded the messy, real-world workflows of the business into a system designed to automate them. It's a level of grounding that's very hard to copy, and you can see it in how naturally the product fits the agencies they acquire.
EQT's track record in services buy-and-build
Finally, this is a playbook EQT knows inside out. Industrialising add-on M&A in fragmented service markets is one of our core strengths, built up across some of our most successful platforms, including IVC Evidensia in veterinary care and Anticimex in pest control, among others.
That means we bring a lot more than capital. We bring a tested approach to sourcing, executing and integrating acquisitions at pace; a network of senior industrial advisors with directly relevant operating experience; and the support to help a young, fast-moving company scale its M&A engine without losing the discipline that makes it work. A demonstrated services buy-and-build partner alongside a category-defining AI-native platform is, we think, what makes EQT well-placed to support Dwelly's next chapter.
We believe AI-native companies like Dwelly represent a new chapter for European technology. The combination of exceptional founders, proprietary operational data and AI-native execution creates a different kind of company: one capable of transforming entire industries rather than simply digitising them.
We're excited to partner with Ilya, Dan, Dmitry and the entire Dwelly team as they build what we believe can become a global category leader.

rows.title: Carolina Brochado on Bloomberg TV: AI, Deep Tech and the Next Generation of Technology Companies

Carolina Brochado on Bloomberg TV: AI, Deep Tech and the Next Generation of Technology Companies
')">

5min read
Carolina Brochado on Bloomberg TV: AI, Deep Tech and the Next Generation of Technology Companies
Carolina Brochado on Bloomberg TV: AI, Deep Tech and the Next Generation of Technology Companies
Authors
EQT Ventures
Artificial intelligence is reshaping industries, accelerating company creation and changing how technology businesses are built. At the same time, Europe is entering a new phase, with stronger founders, deeper technical talent and growing access to long-term growth capital.
Speaking with Dani Burger on
Bloomberg Deals
, Carolina Brochado, Partner and Head of EQT Ventures & EQT Growth US, shared why EQT believes this is one of the most exciting moments for European technology in decades.
AI is creating a much bigger opportunity
While enterprise software has created some of the world's largest technology companies, Carolina believes AI expands the opportunity far beyond software itself.
"The software market is something like $1.2 trillion. AI, if you think about it relative to the services industry, could be a $15 trillion opportunity."
Rather than simply improving existing software, AI is beginning to transform entire service industries. From legal services and customer support to software development, the technology has the potential to unlock significant productivity gains across the economy.
Deep tech's moment has arrived
Long before AI became today's dominant technology trend, EQT Ventures was investing in deep technology across robotics, industrial systems and space.
According to Carolina, those long-term convictions are now converging with a broader shift towards reindustrialisation and sovereign technology capabilities.
"For the last 10 years, we have thought that deep tech is around the corner. Now we are in a nice position with AI and the reindustrialization of everything."
She pointed to portfolio companies including
Starcloud
, building data centres in space, and
The Exploration Company
, developing reusable spacecraft, as examples of technologies benefiting from this new wave of investment and industrial innovation.
Building Europe's next generation of global technology companies
Asked about the newly established
Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT
, Carolina highlighted the importance of addressing one of Europe's longstanding challenges: access to growth-stage capital for deep technology companies.
"There is a clear gap at growth stage for deep tech businesses in Europe. We think this was a fantastic initiative."
She explained that, by combining EQT's venture, growth and life sciences capabilities, the firm is well positioned to support Europe's most ambitious companies as they scale into global technology leaders.
AI will change work, but also create opportunity
The discussion also turned to the impact AI will have on jobs, with companies like Harvey transforming legal work and Lovable making software development accessible to a much broader audience.
Carolina acknowledged that AI will change how many people work but believes the long-term effect will be positive.
As AI automates repetitive tasks, people will increasingly be able to focus on higher-value work, creativity and innovation.
Investing through the next wave
Technology investing has always evolved through cycles. While software defined the last decade, AI, deep tech and industrial technologies are creating entirely new markets and business models.
For EQT, the approach remains consistent: back exceptional founders early, support them over the long term, and help build the next generation of global category-defining companies.

Value Creation: Capturing the AI Opportunity at Scale
Value Creation: Capturing the AI Opportunity at Scale
Authors

At SuperReturn, EQT's Carolina Brochado, Peter Beske Nielsen, Bert Janssens, Hari Gopalakrishnan and Christian Sinding discussed how AI is reshaping value creation across the entire EQT platform, from early-stage venture investments to growth, buyouts and longer-hold strategies.
The central theme was clear: AI is not just a technology trend or an investment category. It is becoming a foundational value creation lever across every sector and every stage of company building.
Carolina Brochado, Head of EQT Ventures and Head of EQT Growth US, highlighted how AI is increasingly touching every corner of the technology landscape.
"What we see now is that AI is really touching every single sub-sector."
That transformation is happening in two ways. First, a new generation of AI-native companies is emerging at unprecedented speed. Carolina pointed to companies such as Lovable, Harvey and Parloa as examples of businesses growing at fast speed compared to previous technology cycles.
"I've never seen so many businesses go from 0 to 10 in less than a year."
Second, existing companies are being transformed through AI adoption. Across the portfolio, businesses are using AI to automate workflows, improve productivity, expand margins and accelerate growth.
Beyond software, EQT is increasingly focused on what Carolina described as "physical AI", AI moving into the real world through robotics and infrastructure. Companies such as 1X demonstrate how AI is evolving from digital applications into physical intelligence, enabling robots to perceive, learn and operate in the real world.
The broader message from the session was that value creation increasingly depends on an organisation's ability to identify, adopt and operationalise AI. For EQT, that means combining investments in promising AI companies with a focus on helping portfolio companies capture the opportunities created by the technology.
The opportunity extends across venture, growth, buyouts and longer-hold strategies alike. AI is no longer a sector. It is becoming a layer across the entire economy.

What a Ride

Today,

When we first invested in 2019, electrification was far from obvious, and Einride's vision felt almost scarily ambitious. From Perk to P&L: Why Wellbeing Defines High-Performing Companies
')">

5min read
From Perk to P&L: Why Wellbeing Defines High-Performing Companies
From Perk to P&L: Why Wellbeing Defines High-Performing Companies
Authors
EQT Ventures
At Transform in Las Vegas, Polly Barnes, Operating Partner Talent at EQT, sat down with Livia Martini, CPO at Wellhub, for a conversation on what it really takes to build high-performance organisations today.
One idea came through clearly: wellbeing is no longer a perk, it’s a core driver of business performance.
Coming from a background in investment banking, consulting, and as a CFO, Livia brings a distinctly operator-led lens to people and culture. Her approach is simple but powerful: treat the People function like any other part of the business, focused on the levers that drive growth. Because ultimately, people are the P&L.
That perspective becomes critical when you look at the data. Burnout is estimated to cost $322bn globally, while nearly 90% of employees say prioritising their wellbeing improves performance. The companies that win are not the ones talking about wellbeing, but the ones building it deliberately into how they operate.
And that’s where many organisations fall short.
There’s a striking disconnect: while 98% of CEOs believe wellbeing has improved, only half of employees agree. The gap isn’t intent, it’s execution. Too often, programmes are designed in a way that doesn’t translate into everyday behaviour, or worse, only work for leadership teams but not the broader organisation.
At Wellhub, the focus has been on making wellbeing part of the cultural fabric, from hiring and communication to leadership behaviour and team rituals. Leaders actively role model it. It shows up in how teams work, how success is celebrated, and how people are supported day-to-day. Not as a side initiative, but as a shared expectation.
Importantly, this isn’t about slowing down performance, it’s about sustaining it.
High-performing environments, especially in fast-growing companies, carry an inherent risk of burnout if left unmanaged. The insight Livia shared is that sustained high performance and wellbeing are not in tension, they reinforce each other. The best teams don’t choose between the two; they build systems where both can exist.
The takeaway is a clear shift in how leading companies think about culture: wellbeing isn’t something you add on top, it’s what everything else is built on.

Building Category Leaders: What Vinted’s €8bn Secondary Transaction Tells Us

We have been extraordinarily fortunate to have had a front-row seat to Vinted's outlier trajectory over the past five years. One of the greatest challenges facing European entrepreneurs is that they must almost always "go international" from day one. Vinted has not only met that challenge, it has built an expansion playbook that has made it stronger. Since our investment, Vinted has successfully expanded into 10+ countries (25+ markets in total), extended beyond fashion into new categories, and built both a shipping and payments business, all while hiring and retaining exceptional talent. In 2025, Vinted surpassed €10bn in GMV, growing close to 50% while continuing to expand profitability.
Given Vinted’s performance and the enormous size of the opportunity ahead, it was no tough choice to decide to double-down on the latest investment opportunity. Vinted is a great example of a technology company building and growing a category through the rare combination of exceptional execution and an entrepreneurial spirit. Pragmatism combined with a very high level of ambition to transform second-hand into our first choice, a noble cause that benefits the planet.
Vinted’s round was €880m in secondary share transactions and extremely oversubscribed. As private companies are staying private for longer the secondary markets are now absorbing billions in supply. With everything happening in AI, including more value accruing to those successfully deploying it, we believe power laws will be compounded with winners becoming even larger. Secondary transactions like this allow companies to provide liquidity to employees and early investors, while continuing to operate with a long-term focus.
At EQT, we mean it when we say we are long-term investors and are extremely excited to continue to partner with giants like Vinted. The opportunity ahead remains significant. Second-hand commerce continues to grow, supported by shifts in consumer behaviour, sustainability, and cost awareness. With its unique and scaled marketplace, supported by its logistics and payments businesses, Vinted is uniquely positioned to continue compounding and grow at scale for years to come.

On a Mission to Make First Contact with Superintelligence

On a Mission to Make First Contact with Superintelligence
On a Mission to Make First Contact with Superintelligence
Authors
Sandra Malmberg
Ted Persson
Saiteja Sriramagiri
Hampus Särnbratt
There is something strange about the current path to AI.
We are trying to build systems that exceed human intelligence by training them on what humans have already produced. The training signal is us. So is much of the shape of the system. That path has worked astonishingly well. Internet-scale training has turned the accumulated record of human language, code, science, argument, and culture into a new kind of machine intelligence.
But evolution took a different route.
There was no pre-existing intelligence to imitate. Agents acting in the world, with survival as the feedback. Across billions of years, that loop produced minds that can discover mathematics on roughly twenty watts of glucose.
Maybe intelligence does not have to begin by imitating intelligence.
Ineffable Intelligence is built around that question. What if the next frontier is not a larger model trained on more of the human record, but a superlearner that discovers knowledge from its own experience? A system that begins with elementary motor skills, learns by doing, and gradually builds its own understanding of the world. One that can rediscover language, science, mathematics, and technology, and then move beyond the limits of what humans happened to write down.
David Silver has been pushing this frontier for decades: Atari from pixels, AlphaGo, AlphaZero, systems that learned chess, shogi, and Go through self-play, and later work contributing to AlphaFold and AlphaProof. Reduce the human scaffold. Let the system learn from experience. See how far it can go.
If this works, it would suggest that intelligence has a deeper, more general structure. Darwin gave us a law for life. The hope here is a companion law for intelligence -- one that can both explain it, and build it.
We are proud to support Ineffable Intelligence as part of their $1.1 billion seed round, alongside Sequoia Capital, Lightspeed, Index Ventures, NVIDIA, Google, DST Global, Wellcome Trust, Bond Capital, British Business Bank, Flying Fish Partners, Evantic Capital, Sovereign AI Fund, and a group of thoughtful angels.
Some ideas expand the frontier a little.
Others ask whether the frontier itself is in the right place.
We’re excited to see how Ineffable reshapes what’s possible.

rows.title: Natural Cycles: How Elina Berglund and Raoul Scherwitzl developed the world’s first digital contraceptive
rows.text:
Natural Cycles: How Elina Berglund and Raoul Scherwitzl developed the world’s first digital contraceptive
')">
Apr 1, 2026
5min read
Natural Cycles: How Elina Berglund and Raoul Scherwitzl developed the world’s first digital contraceptive
Natural Cycles: How Elina Berglund and Raoul Scherwitzl developed the world’s first digital contraceptive
Authors
EQT Ventures
Natural Cycles co-founders Dr. Elina Berglund and Dr. Raoul Scherwitzl, a real-life husband and wife team, are transforming contraception with their innovative digital approach.
The couple first crossed paths at UC Santa Barbara, in what Raoul describes romantically as a moment straight from a Richard Curtis film: “Our hands grazed as we reached for the same textbook from opposite sides of the bookshelf; our eyes locked and in that moment…we just knew.” Elina offers a less cinematic version: “We were probably just sitting around a table doing our physics homework.”
Years later, and on a different continent, they would start Natural Cycles, the world’s first digital, non-hormonal, and non-invasive contraception. At the time, Elina was engaged in the small matter of searching for the Higgs boson at CERN, assisting with work that would later be awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics, whilst Raoul was undertaking a PhD in Condensed Matter and Materials Physics.
The idea came about in the summer of 2012; the couple had recently got married and were looking for a natural method of contraception.
“We wanted to have kids within a couple of years,” explains Elina, “and I was looking for a non-hormonal form of contraception. I couldn’t find the right solution anywhere. I had access to a number of scientific publications and started to read about how body temperature changes throughout your cycle. I started tinkering, creating the very first version of the Natural Cycles algorithm just to use myself.”
The two quickly realised that this algorithm addressed an as-yet unmet need: a birth control method by which women could track their cycles in a non-hormonal and non-invasive way. Six months later, they had quit their jobs to focus on developing the company.
With two PhDs between them, building the product was the easy part.
“As scientists, we were both trained to analyze data and write code. The difficulty came in understanding regulation and marketing the product. That’s where we had to find help,” explains Raoul.
“There is this scary moment when you start to hire people to the company you started,” continues Raoul, “where you think, ‘Ok, it’s not just consumers - I now have a responsibility to other people to make this company a success."
Without a background in business, the early days contained a lot of learning and navigation for the couple.
“We solved problems one-by-one”, says Elina. “We knew that the product worked, but we had to prove it clinically. This is a serious company with serious consequences, and we knew that we couldn’t necessarily ‘move fast and break things."
This is the mantra of many startups, but anyone familiar with regulatory processes, especially those in America, knows that it is often a treacle-like process. “Moving fast” and government-level regulation rarely go hand-in-hand.
“The European CE-marking and the FDA-clearance were both incredibly important milestones in the company”, says Raoul. “I was in the supermarket when I got the email confirming FDA-clearance. It was a funny moment of being in an incredibly mundane environment whilst receiving completely groundbreaking news. Like, ‘Oh, our company now has a certified future in helping women and families worldwide. Also, we need milk."
A month later, the couple moved to New York.
As the first product of its kind, which still remains the only certified digital contraception in the US and Europe, Natural Cycles inevitably invoked skepticism from incumbent pharmaceutical companies that were wary of the new kids on the block.
“There was a lot of doubt cast on us when we were growing,” says Raoul. “It took some time to establish ourselves on the market and become recognised enough for consumers to recognise that we are a viable alternative to contraceptive pills and condoms.”
In the early days, there were instances where skepticism became criticism. Negative publicity is difficult to navigate for any company at any stage, but especially so for a young startup recently launched in a new market.
Elina is contemplative about it.
“It was clear from the start that this is a product that women want and therefore needs to be on the market,” she explains. “There was no other effective solution to natural contraception and that made it so obvious that we needed to stick with it. We’re both extremely resilient, so there was never a doubt in our minds that we would capitulate.”
It was precisely this resilience that attracted EQT Ventures to the company. By the time EQT Ventures led the company’s Series B funding round in 2017, Natural Cycles had already demonstrated both scientific credibility and strong early market traction.
Today, Carolina Brochado, Partner and Head of EQT Ventures, sits on the company’s board.
“When you look at the Natural Cycles story, what stands out is the founders’ tenacity,” says Carolina. “Building a company at the intersection of healthcare, regulation and consumer technology requires an unusual level of resilience, discipline and building for the long-term. Elina and Raoul have demonstrated both.”
EQT Ventures has worked closely with the company for years as it scaled globally.
“Natural Cycles is a great example of a company that created an entirely new category,” Carolina continues. “Digital contraception did not exist before they built it, and bringing that to market required scientific rigor, regulatory breakthroughs and a willingness to challenge a very established industry.”
Wearables integration would later prove to be a major inflection point for the company.
“That phase required patience,” explains Elina. “Scaling a regulated healthcare product globally takes time, and EQT Ventures stayed supportive through that period. That’s exactly what you want from an investor.”
Wearable integration was far from inevitable, though.
“I wish we could say that we knew it was going to happen,” says Elina, “But really we just spent a lot of time saying, ‘Oh, imagine if the Apple Watch had a temperature sensor’. And then it got one.”
As Natural Cycles has grown, so has the scope of the company’s work. What began as a software algorithm has evolved into a broader reproductive health platform that now also includes hardware, such as the NC° Band and integrations with wearable devices like the Oura Ring and Apple Watch.
Moving from pure software into hardware-enabled solutions has allowed the company to make fertility tracking more seamless and accessible for millions of users around the world.
With this growth has also come a larger role in shaping the broader conversation around women’s health.
As the company has scaled globally, Natural Cycles increasingly engages on a societal and policy level. In Sweden, for example, the company is actively advocating for fairer regulation for women’s health, including campaigning against the high and unequal VAT placed on non-prescription birth control.
What started as a scientific innovation has grown into a company working to improve not only technology, but also the structural conditions around reproductive healthcare.
Despite soaring user uptake, operating in over 160 countries, three funding rounds, and Elina being named Entrepreneur of the Year 2025 by Dagens Industri’s “Sweden’s Most Powerful Women in Business”, the couple still see these as early days for the company.
“Like every software company, AI is revolutionizing our models,” states Elina. “We’re so excited about how it is accelerating our algorithms, and LLM models have amazing potential for the UX of the platform.”
Carolina agrees.
“The potential market for Natural Cycles remains enormous,” she says. “It’s rare to see a company combine deep science, global regulatory approval and consumer adoption in this way. Elina and Raoul have built something truly category-defining, and we believe the journey is still in its early chapters.”

rows.title: Carolina Brochado on CNBC: Europe’s Moment in AI, Capital, and the Future of Software
rows.text:
Carolina Brochado on CNBC: Europe’s Moment in AI, Capital, and the Future of Software
')">
Mar 31, 2026
5min read
Carolina Brochado on CNBC: Europe’s Moment in AI, Capital, and the Future of Software
Carolina Brochado on CNBC: Europe’s Moment in AI, Capital, and the Future of Software
Authors
EQT Ventures
Last week, Carolina Brochado, Head of EQT Ventures, joined CNBC’s
Squawk Box Europe
in conversation with Ritika Gupta to discuss Europe’s position in the global tech race, and why the opportunity is far from lost.
Below is a snapshot of the key themes from the discussion.
Is Europe falling behind in tech, or is the opportunity still ahead?
Carolina’s view is clear: Europe remains a uniquely strong environment for building technology companies. The region combines world-class academic institutions with a long history of producing category-defining businesses, from DeepMind to Revolut.
What’s changing now is the urgency. As AI reshapes industries, Europe has a renewed opportunity to compete, particularly in areas where it already has structural strengths.
What’s holding Europe back today?
The core constraint remains capital.
While Europe has a thriving early-stage ecosystem, there is still a significant gap at the growth and IPO stages. Many companies continue to look abroad,  particularly to the US,  for deeper capital markets and more attractive listing environments.
But it’s not just about funding. Europe’s fragmentation adds operational complexity, with companies scaling across multiple languages, regulatory systems, and markets from day one.
At the same time, this has shaped a different kind of founder.
Do these constraints create stronger companies?
In many ways, yes.
European founders are often forced to think globally earlier, operate with tighter capital discipline, and build with a sharper focus on unit economics. When companies from Europe do scale, they tend to do so with more resilient and efficient growth models.
Where can Europe win in AI?
While much of the AI conversation has focused on large-scale models and infrastructure, Carolina highlighted Europe’s edge in what she described as “physical AI”, applications rooted in the real world.
With a deep industrial base and strong research institutions, Europe is well positioned in areas like robotics, energy systems, and advanced manufacturing. Companies like
1X
, EQT’s Norwegian portfolio company building humanoid robots, are early examples of this shift from purely digital AI to embodied intelligence.
Is AI disrupting software, and are moats disappearing?
The impact of AI on software is more nuanced than the “software is dead” narrative suggests.
What is clear is that some traditional moats are weakening. The speed and cost of building software have decreased dramatically, making it easier to replicate features and products.
However, not all defensibility is disappearing. Carolina pointed to proprietary data and network effects as enduring advantages. In this new landscape, value is shifting, from how quickly you can build, to what you uniquely control and how deeply you are embedded in workflows.
What needs to change for Europe to build trillion-dollar companies?
According to Carolina, it’s not a question of talent or ambition, both are already present.
The gap lies in capital formation across all stages, particularly at scale, and in creating an environment where companies can grow and operate more seamlessly. This includes everything from deeper capital markets to more flexible frameworks for hiring, incentivising, and scaling teams.
A defining moment for European tech
Despite geopolitical uncertainty, the broader tone was one of optimism.
AI represents a structural shift, not just a technological one, but an opportunity to reshape where and how global companies are built. For Europe, the ingredients are already there. The challenge now is execution.
As Carolina put it, the opportunity is not behind us, it’s happening now.

rows.title: Rethinking Marketplaces Beyond Matchmaking
rows.text:
Rethinking Marketplaces Beyond Matchmaking
')">
Mar 20, 2026
5min read
Rethinking Marketplaces Beyond Matchmaking
Rethinking Marketplaces Beyond Matchmaking
Authors
Conrad Schoo
Rania Belkahia
We backed some of the defining marketplaces of the last decade. Handshake built one of the largest early talent networks in the US, fundamentally changing how a generation of students access opportunity and how employers find their next hire. Wolt turned food delivery into a premium consumer experience across dozens of markets, and became one of Europe's most celebrated exits. Vinted redefined second-hand commerce at global scale, building one of the most efficient and trusted peer-to-peer marketplaces in the world. We know what a great marketplace looks like. And right now, something is shifting.
The old marketplace model has been under pressure
The first wave of internet marketplaces created enormous value, but the underlying economics were always fragile. Customer acquisition was expensive, retention was hard as buyers and sellers learned to transact directly, and take rates stayed thin because the core product, pure matching, was difficult to defend. The model worked when custom curation and network effects were strong enough to carry the business. The best platforms built trusted, vetted supply that buyers couldn't easily replicate elsewhere. That curation edge can now be run better and faster at close to zero marginal cost, leaving legacy platforms exposed to disruption risk.
From matchmaker to operator
The new generation of marketplaces must go beyond curation and matchmaking. They draft the proposal, score the candidates, benchmark the price, and run the compliance check. The platform is now embedded in the transaction itself, and goes beyond a simple introduction.
The degree of embedding varies, and so does the resulting platform stickiness. At one end, pure brokers match supply and demand, leading to high disintermediation risk and thin moats. At the other end, embedded platforms run the customer's core operations, making churn nearly impossible. Financing and white-label models sit in between, each trading off brand risk or underwriting complexity for greater lock-in.
EQT view - Four marketplace archetypes by integration level and stickiness
Instead of taking a cut of GMV, these platforms often charge for outcomes: a hire made, a tender won, a shipment cleared. And the competitive dynamic shifts too. The real alternative is no longer another platform, but the internal team or process the customer has been running themselves.
New moats, new economics
Traditional marketplace models were typically constrained by a supply-demand-mismatch, where liquidity became a key value proposition. Get enough buyers and sellers in one place and the platform becomes hard to displace. With the new generation of marketplaces, every transaction accelerates supply build-out via AI-assisted onboarding, improves buyer-seller matchmaking, and raises the costs of churning from the platform.
The resulting unit economics also look different. When a platform handles execution end to end, buyers and sellers have far less reason to bypass it; disintermediation becomes harder and logo retention improves. Automated intake and more precise matchmaking also reduce the cost of acquiring and activating new participants. Lower CAC, lower churn, and higher repeat usage compound into an LTV:CAC ratio that the first generation of marketplaces rarely achieved.
Where we see new models emerging
AI is unlocking entirely new business models in markets that have been waiting for a better solution. We are actively looking at opportunities like these:
Recruiting and talent.
Sourcing, screening, and running interviews autonomously, charging for the hire rather than the listing. The whole recruitment process becomes a managed service.
Public tenders.
Billions in public contracts go uncaptured every year because the process of finding, evaluating, and responding to tenders is operationally heavy. A platform that scans continuously, scores relevance, and drafts the bid turns this into an accessible market for the first time.
Logistics and freight.
Beyond connecting shippers and carriers, handling routing, exceptions, and customs documentation in real time. The platform compounds on routing decisions, exception handling, and carrier performance data.
SMB insurance
: Handling risk assessment, policy sourcing, and claims coordination and compounds on loss data over time.
Skilled trades
: Enabling lead qualification, job scoping, materials procurement, and payment for plumbers, electricians, and contractors.
Healthcare operations.
Matching on outcomes, availability, and patient need to bring consistency and speed to healthcare ops.
If you're building the next generation of marketplaces, we want to hear from you!
